chapter: Joining Goodman and views on arranging
title: George Handy and the unplayed adventurous scores
summary: He wrote experimental pieces for McKinley and others that were never played.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: In that Metronome interview, it is interesting, especially for me since I had that involvement with that Boyd Raeburn project recently, you mention in there that George Handy, who at the time was writing for the Raeburn band and was doing really, quite a few adventurous things, you mentioned that he was doing the things for Boyd that you'd really not had a chance to do with the bands that you worked with.
Right. I did them for McKinley, but he didn't play them either. Not those. They didn't even do them in Sauter-Finegan.
I guess the occasion didn't arise. It was not commercial stuff.
I did get to use it in that festival with the German band I had. They didn't like it either.
It was then already ten years later.

(Inaudible) That's the way it was going. And of course Alexander's big mouth was always involved with Ray McKinley too. The agent was telling him what to play, and telling me how to write. I wanted to go that way, my instincts wanted to go that way and I was always held back because the environment was not right.

I'm not entirely against that sort of thing because I think the conditioning of how you live has an awful lot to do with the band you were playing, if there is any value at all in what you do. Nothing is

done by the individual per se, it's always a result of a mixture-a social mix. The talent has to be there but it's a variable way, depending on how the environment is working with you. I think that's true of everybody involved with anybody that has to do with this sort of thing.
